examples: I cannot help being moved by his courageous act.
I cannot contain my anger at the string of scandals.
Witnessing the devastation in the disaster area firsthand, I cannot hold back a sorrow beyond words.
I cannot help being astonished by his irresponsible remarks.
This ruling is fair, and at the same time I cannot help feeling relieved.
fields.explain:
Attaches only to emotion nouns; does not go directly with verbs/adjectives.
Usually placed at the end of a sentence; what comes before states the situation that causes the emotion.
Stronger and more formal than ないではいられない／ずにはいられない (which are used with verbs).

• Cannot hold back / cannot help feeling N (a strong emotion) in the face of some situation.
• Written, formal nuance; often used in commentary, newspaper articles, and speeches.
• The subject is a person or group acting as the speaker/observer; rarely used with an inanimate subject.
fields.notes:
• Sino-Japanese emotion nouns give a serious feel: 憤り、憤怒、落胆、羞恥、感嘆、悲嘆...
• To emphasize the degree, you can add 割り切れない思い/やりきれない思いなど and then use ～を禁じ得ない.
• In critiques/editorials, this phrase helps make the writing more objective and coherent.
mistakes: Using it with a verb: incorrect. It must be an emotion noun.
Inanimate subject (会社、この結果など) + を禁じ得ない: unnatural. The subject should be a person/group of people.
Confusing it with ～ずにはいられない: exam questions ask about the difference in the type of word it attaches to and the level of formality.

<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>わないではいられない。
Slightly more formal than ～ないではいられない
<ruby>涙<rt>なみだ</rt></ruby>せずにはいられない。
Not an emotion; circumstances force it
<ruby>撤退<rt>てったい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>余儀<rt>よぎ</rt></ruby>なくされる。

examples: After repeated prototyping, we finally managed to bring it to market.
After a rigorous review, the certification was obtained.
After long negotiations, the two parties reached a settlement.
Building on previous research, a new hypothesis was presented.
Via social media, the information spread instantly.
fields.explain:
Usually attaches to time nouns/nouns of stages (年月、期間、準備、交渉、審査、試験運用...).
Formal, objective style; suited to administrative/technical documents.
To emphasize "throughout a period of time," consider ～を通じて/～を通して; to emphasize "through a channel," you can use ～を経由して, but ～を経て is more formal.

• Expresses "going through" a period of time/process/stage/intermediate channel, which then leads to a later result.
• Official nuance; used in reports, press releases, histories of development, and descriptions of procedures.
• Emphasizes accumulation/sequential progress through several steps before reaching a result.
fields.notes:
• “経る(へる)” suggests a verified process/intermediate step: 試験運用→本格運用, パイロット→ローンチ.
• Goes well with 至る・実現する・承認される・完成する to emphasize the result achieved.
• In histories/summaries of events, a sequence like “創業→拡大→再編→上場” is often described with ～を経て.
mistakes: Misreading “へて” as “えて”: incorrect. The kanji 経 is read へ(る).
Using it for an instantaneous event with no process: inappropriate. Choose ～を通じて／経由して depending on the context.
Confusing it with ～の末（に）: “の末” has an emotional coloring of a final outcome, while “を経て” is neutral and procedural.

rows: <ruby>交渉<rt>こうしょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>経<rt>へ</rt></ruby>て<ruby>合意<rt>ごうい</rt></ruby>。
～を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて／を<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して
<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて leans toward “throughout,” <ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して toward “by means of” (less formal)
<ruby>一年<rt>いちねん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>温暖<rt>おんだん</rt></ruby>だ。メディアを<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して<ruby>発信<rt>はっしん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>香港<rt>ほんこん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>経由<rt>けいゆ</rt></ruby>して<ruby>出荷<rt>しゅっか</rt></ruby>。
Emphasizes the outcome after a lot of effort; emotional nuance
<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>末<rt>すえ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>結論<rt>けつろん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>達<rt>たっ</rt></ruby>した。

examples: We will review our sales strategy based on the latest statistics.
Present a hypothesis that builds on previous research.
Taking all of your feedback into account, we will improve our service.
Taking legal precedents into account, a settlement proposal was presented.
The plan was revised based on the results of the field survey.
fields.explain:
Serious and objective; often appears in reports, proposals, research papers, and official statements.
Often combines with verbs meaning adjust/decide:見直す,決定する,設計する,立案する,判断する,改善する,策定する.
Can come at the beginning of a sentence to state the basis, followed by the main action.
Not used for purely emotional opinions; there should be a concrete/objective "basis" involved.

• Based on, taking … as the basis for deciding/evaluating/proposing.
• Implies "having carefully considered" data/facts/precedents before acting; formal nuance, common in academic, business, and administrative contexts.
• Different from "rough reference": ～を踏まえて implies a firm foundation (a basis that carries weight).
• Often used with nouns such as: データ, 結果, 実績, 事実, 判例, ご意見, 先行研究, 反省, 需要動向, 市況, ガイドライン.
fields.notes:
• “踏まえる” originally means "to step on" → metaphor of "standing on a foundation (basis)."
• In emails/minutes: “ご指摘を踏まえまして～” is very natural and polite.
• When the basis is highly quantitative, you can use ～に基づいて instead to emphasize standardization.
meaning_vi: ～を前提(ぜんてい)、根拠(こんきょ)として→考(かんが)える、作成(さくせい)する
Based on
力(ちから)を入(い)れて踏(ふ)む
examples: 1. 先行研究を踏まえて論文を書く。
Write a thesis based on previous research.
2. 「今回の失敗を踏まえて、次はどうすべきかを考えてみます」
Based on this failure, let's think about what we should do next time.
3. 会議では前回までの議論を踏まえて、さらに内容を深めた話し合いが行われた。
At the meeting, a discussion was held that deepened the content further, building on the discussions up to the previous meeting.
4. 両足で大地を踏まえて立つ。
Step firmly on the ground with both feet.
mistakes: Use it for an objective basis; avoid using it with vague personal feelings (× 気分を踏まえて決める).
Confusing it with ～をもとに when you mean "adapt/create" (films, stories) → use ～をもとに.
The JLPT often asks you to distinguish を踏まえて vs に基づいて vs をもとに; note the "careful consideration" nuance of を踏まえて.

examples: As of today, I'm giving up sweets.
This series will end with the next issue.
Our store will close at the end of this month.
He announced that he would retire after this season.
Applications for this project close today.
fields.explain:
Formal; suited to notices and official statements.
Often used with verbs such as: やめる,終了する,閉店する,打ち切る,引退する,打ち切り,打ち止め.
The emphasis is on the "final point in time," unlike a plain "from now on."

• "With … as the last time / at the end of …, something stops/no longer continues."
• Emphasizes that a point in time is the boundary at which an action/state ends.
• Often used in declarations, press releases, personal resolutions, or organizational announcements.
• Typical accompanying words: 今日, 今回, 今月, 今季, 今年, 本日, 今号, 次回, 〇月末, 〇年度 など.
fields.notes:
• In everyday spoken language, speakers often use 今日で/今月で instead of ～を限りに to sound softer.
• Notice boards/posters prefer “N 限りで” or “N をもちまして” (very formal).
mistakes: Use it with nouns of "time/period"; avoid nouns that are not about time (× 気分を限りにやめる).
Confusing it with “N までに” (deadline) → ～を限りに means "last time/ending," not "deadline for completion."
The JLPT often asks about the set ～を限りに vs 限りで vs をもちまして in the context of announcements.

fields.connection: Vない(drop ない) + んがため(に)・んがための + N (exception: しない→せん)
examples: He repeatedly took on reckless challenges in order to gain fame.
In order to survive, the company pushed through large-scale restructuring.
She blew the whistle in order to bring the truth to light.
He worked out a strategy for winning down to the last detail.
The refugees headed for the border in order to escape the war.
fields.explain:
Has a determined, "at all costs" nuance. Used to emphasize a strong motive or the legitimacy (or reprehensibility) of an action.
Often appears with heavy vocabulary:無謀,極端,決行,犠牲,断行…
Not used for natural/objective purposes (e.g., "so as not to miss the train" usually takes ～ように/ために).
Placed before a noun as ～んがための + N to highlight "for the purpose of X."

- Meaning: "in order to (achieve at all costs) …"; expresses a purpose with extremely strong volition, sometimes with a "regardless of anything" nuance.
• Emphasizes an intense, determined motive, much stronger than ～ために, ～ように.
• Often used with purposes of great value (victory, fame, survival…), sometimes leading to excessive actions.
• The subject of the purpose clause and the main clause is usually the same intentional agent.
• Style: formal, written language, speeches, history; not used for daily life or small purposes.
• Not used with direct command/request sentences.
fields.notes:
• “せんがため” is the classical form of “する” used in this structure; it is not the negative “しない.”
• For 来る, the classical form “こんがため” exists but is rare; avoid it in exam prep and use a substitute verb (来訪す, 訪れる…).
• In literature/speeches, this pattern is often placed at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize the purpose.
mistakes: Wrong subject: the purpose clause and the main clause must have the same intentional agent.
Using it for trivial matters: × 時間を節約せんがために早起きする → use ～ために/～ように.
Mistaking “せん” for a negative: “せんがため” ≠ “しないため”.
Attaching it to a request sentence: × 合格せんがために手伝ってください → clash of nuance.
Confusing it with “～がために” (cause): distinguish the meaning "purpose" vs "because of (negative)."

rows: Neutral, widely used; does not necessarily imply strong volition
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>するために<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
Does not emphasize volition; used with ability, machines, phenomena
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れないように<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る
Formal but milder than ～んがために
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>すべく<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>した
Same form, but means "because" when it is a reason clause
<ruby>貧<rt>まず</rt></ruby>しいがために<ruby>進学<rt>しんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>断念<rt>だんねん</rt></ruby>した

fields.connection: Vない(drop ない) + んばかり(に)・んばかりの + N (exception: しない→せん)
examples: He was so happy he was almost in tears.
He apologized, practically pressing his head to the floor.
The hall was filled with thunderous applause.
My heart feels as if it is about to burst.
The water has been poured so full that the glass is about to overflow.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker judges that something is "about to" happen, though in reality it usually has not happened; leans toward exaggerating an impression.
Suited to literary descriptions, newspaper articles, and storytelling; rarely used in ordinary conversation.
Not used for ordinary objective events (×早起き んばかりに 起きた).

- Meaning: "to the point of being about to …," "as if … at any moment"; emphasizes an extremely high degree, though it usually has not actually happened.
• Describes an outward state/image that makes the speaker "feel as if" something is about to happen.
• Often used with strong emotions and gestures: 泣く, 叫ぶ, 壊れる, 溢れる, 飛び出す…
• Slightly more literary/formal style than ～ほど/～くらい.
fields.notes:
• Very common set phrases: 割れんばかりの拍手, 溢れんばかりの笑顔／花, 飛び出さんばかりの勢い.
• “せんばかり” for する is a classical form; do not confuse it with the negative.
• Often used with a noun + の as a modifier: ～んばかりのN makes the sentence more natural.
mistakes: Describing something that actually happened: × 泣いんばかりに泣いた → redundant; use ほど/くらい.
Attaching it to everyday objective actions → does not fit the nuance.
Confusing it with ばかりだ (tendency) in JLPT questions; note the different semantic field.
Choosing the wrong verb: prefer vivid verbs/phrases with strong emotion.

rows: Neutral, widely used; no literary nuance
<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>きたいほど<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しい
Hypothetical comparison; not necessarily "about to" happen
<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>砂糖<rt>さとう</rt></ruby>であるかのように<ruby>白<rt>しろ</rt></ruby>い
Emphasizes a gesture/action as if wanting to say something
<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていたとばかりに<ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す
Different meaning: shows only an upward/downward trend

examples: He's an amateur, but he has the knowledge of a professional.
This year's cold is about the same as usual.
This smartphone's camera takes pictures as good as a DSLR's.
I just want to live a normal life like everyone else.
At Tokyo-level rents, you can't rent anything in the provinces.
fields.explain:
Usually placed before a noun to state the "standard of comparison."
“人並み” is used to mean the "ordinary level, like other people," sometimes implying modesty.
With “例年並み/平年並み”: expresses an average level over many years.

• "A degree equivalent to/like N"; emphasizes "being on a par with the standard/object of comparison."
• Can have a positive meaning (reaching a high standard: プロ並み) or a neutral one (例年並み), depending on the context.
• Unlike ほど/くらい (estimation), 並み leans toward "a truly equal standard."
• Often used with standards such as: プロ, 大人, 人, 世界, 一流, 例年, 平年, 都会, 東京, 外資, 欧米, 最新.
fields.notes:
• “A 並みの B” → B reaches the standard of A; “A 並みに C” → C happens at a level like A.
• “世界並み” is sometimes translated as "meeting international standards."
• In business, “大手並みの待遇/福利厚生” is a very common phrase.
mistakes: Confusing it with ほど/くらい: ～並み emphasizes an "equivalent standard," not just a vague estimate.
Do not use ～並み for comparisons of more/less (× A は B 並みより上). Rephrase as: “A は B 並みかそれ以上”.
The JLPT often tests swapping: プロ並みの vs プロほど（に）は～ない → different nuances.

rows: On a par with, at the same level
<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby><ruby>記録<rt>きろく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>匹敵<rt>ひってき</rt></ruby>する
プロ<ruby>級<rt>きゅう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>選手<rt>せんしゅ</rt></ruby>

examples: When you come to Tokyo, please be sure to stop by our office.
Thank you for attending the other day despite your busy schedule.
When I came to Japan, I met up with some old friends again.
When I went on a business trip to Osaka, I also stopped by the head office.
On this occasion, I would like to express my deep gratitude for everyone's support.
I talked a little with Professor Mori at the party the other day.
fields.explain:
More formal than とき/際に; often found in emails, company notices, and speeches.
Used with “には” when inserting an invitation/suggestion: ～折には、ぜひ…
Works with both the past (Vた) and a planned future (Vる), as long as the "occasion" is fairly specific.

- Meaning: "on the occasion of/when …"; equivalent to ～とき but formal, often used in letters, invitations, and announcements.
• Often used with keigo/refined expressions: お越しの折に, お忙しい折に恐れ入りますが…
• Used for a specific occasion (past/expected), not a hypothetical condition.
• Suited to invitations/politeness: ～折には、ぜひ…ください.
fields.notes:
• “折（おり）” originally means "point in time/opportunity"; mainly written language, and in speech it is usually replaced with とき.
• Common email openers: お忙しい折に恐縮ですが／恐れ入りますが…
• “この折” is used to sum up/thank/change the topic in speeches. meaning_vi: On the occasion of, when, at the time ～ ⏐ explain: Since it means "on some good occasion," the following clause usually does not mention bad things. ⏐ examples: 1. 来日の折には、ぜひこちらにお立ち寄りください。
When you come to Japan, be sure to drop by and see me.
2. 次にお目にかかった折に、お借りしていた本をお返しします。
I'll return the book I borrowed when we meet next time.
mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds "too stiff"; use とき.
Using it for a vague hypothetical condition: × 雨なら折に → wrong semantic field.
Confusing it with 際に in regulations: 際に leans toward rules/clauses; 折に toward letters/speeches.
Dropping “には” in invitations: ～折には is more natural than ～折に in an invitation.

rows: <ruby>暇<rt>ひま</rt></ruby>なとき<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>してください

examples: I am truly grateful for your support.
The results fell short of expectations, which is extremely disappointing.
I'm so happy to hear about my friend's success.
The extent of the damage from the disaster is truly heartbreaking.
I am so relieved to know they are safe overseas.
fields.explain:
Expresses a strong, polite emotional evaluation; suited to formal contexts.
Not used for purely objective descriptions (temperature, figures...).
Avoid applying it directly to other people's emotions when not making a conjecture.

- Used to emphasize a subjective emotion at its peak: "extremely/very/… utterly."
- More formal than とても/本当に; common in speeches, letters, and formal news.
- Mainly used for the speaker's current emotion or after hearing news/an event.
fields.notes:
• Common in business style: 嬉しい限り／ありがたい限り carry a humble, polite tone.
• To sound more casual, switch to とても/本当に + Adj to be natural in conversation.
• In the news, it is used to express emotion about a sad event: 痛ましい限りだ／悲しい限りだ.
mistakes: Confusing it with “～限り” (as long as/the more ~): the two patterns have different functions.
Using it with non-emotional content: (x) 売上は高い限りだ → (o) 非常に高い.
Applying it to other people: (x) 彼は嬉しい限りだ → replace with 彼は嬉しそうだ／嬉しいに違いない when making a conjecture.

<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>
